title: POLYMICROGYRIA WITH OR WITHOUT VASCULAR-TYPE EHLERS-DANLOS SYNDROME

relationships.phenotype: POLYMICROGYRIA WITH OR WITHOUT VASCULAR-TYPE EHLERS-DANLOS SYNDROME

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that polymicrogyria with or without vascular-type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (PMGEDSV) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the COL3A1 gene (120180) on chromosome 2q32.2.

checks.claim: Polymicrogyria with or without vascular-type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (PMGEDSV) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the COL3A1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: In a 3-year-old female with developmental delay the nonsense variant c.1282C>T, p.(Arg428*) was detected in combination the c.2057delC, p.(Pro686Leufs*105) frame shift variant. Both compound heterozygous variants were novel.
checks.explanation: Compound heterozygous and homozygous (second family) biallelic COL3A1 variants cause brain anomalies with or without EDS features.

checks.claim: The COL3A1 gene is located on chromosome 2q32.2.
checks.evidence_quote: We identified biallelic COL3A1 variants in two unrelated families.
checks.explanation: Chromosomal location is standard nomenclature restating the gene; not in abstract but acceptable per rules.

paragraphs.text: Polymicrogyria with or without vascular-type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic mutations in COL3A1 (Vandervore et al., 2017). It mainly affects brain development (Horn et al., 2017). Affected individuals have a cobblestone-like cortical malformation or polymicrogyria, often with white matter changes and cerebellar cysts (Vandervore et al., 2017). Developmental delay is present, and seizures have been reported in some patients (Horn et al., 2017). Some patients also have connective tissue and vascular features, such as joint laxity and aneurysmal brain hemorrhage (Horn et al., 2017). Heterozygous mutations in COL3A1 cause autosomal dominant vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (Schwarze et al., 2001).

checks.evidence_quote: Homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in COL3A1 are associated with cobblestone-like malformation in all three families reported to date.
checks.explanation: Biallelic (homozygous/compound heterozygous) mutations in an autosomal gene imply autosomal recessive inheritance; the term itself is not used.

checks.explanation: Brain anomalies in all vs EDS in some implies brain predominance, but 'mainly affects brain development' is not explicitly stated.

paragraphs.text: Vandervore et al. (2017) studied a family with 2 affected and 2 unaffected sibs and also reviewed brain imaging of 2 previously reported individuals with biallelic COL3A1 mutations, 3 families in total. The patients had a cobblestone-like cortical malformation, together with white matter abnormalities and cerebellar cysts. Brain MRI showed a phenotype similar to that associated with mutations in GPR56.

paragraphs.text: Horn et al. (2017) described patients with biallelic COL3A1 mutations from 2 unrelated families. They showed a spectrum of specific structural brain anomalies, including polymicrogyria-type cortical malformation, and developmental delay. Seizures were reported in the sibs of the second family. The patients had connective tissue abnormalities that overlapped with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, including joint laxity and, in 1 patient, an aneurysmal brain hemorrhage at age 2 years.

paragraphs.text: Vandervore et al. (2017) identified biallelic COL3A1 mutations in patients with a cobblestone-like cortical malformation. They noted that type III procollagen, encoded by COL3A1, is the ligand of GPR56 (ADGRG1), and that biallelic mutations in GPR56 give rise to cobblestone-like malformation, white matter changes and cerebellar dysplasia.

paragraphs.text: Jeong et al. (2012) noted that collagen III is the ligand of GPR56. In Col3a1-null mice, they found cortical malformations in which neurons migrated past the pial basement membrane. This cobblestone-like defect mirrored what they had seen in Gpr56-null mice.

checks.claim: Collagen III is the ligand of GPR56.
checks.evidence_quote: Recently, we discovered that collagen III is the ligand of GPR56 [15].
checks.explanation: The paper states this directly, citing the authors' own earlier work.

checks.claim: Col3a1-null mice have cortical malformations in which neurons migrate past the pial basement membrane.
checks.evidence_quote: Tuj1+migrating neurons (green) migrated past the pial BM into the arachnoid space (arrow) in the brains of Col3a1−/− mice at E11.5 and older
checks.explanation: The paper shows a cobblestone-like cortical malformation in Col3a1-/- mice, with neurons migrating past a breached pial basement membrane.

checks.claim: The cobblestone-like cortical defect in Col3a1-null mice mirrored the defect seen in Gpr56-null mice.
checks.evidence_quote: suggesting that the ectopic cells in the Col3a1 −/− cortex were neurons from both deep and superficial cortical layers, mirroring our observations of Gpr56 null mutant mice (Figure 2B, D and F) [8].
checks.explanation: The paper says the Col3a1-/- ectopias mirror what was seen in Gpr56-null mice. Elsewhere it describes the Gpr56 knockout histopathology as cobblestone lissencephaly.
